clue.text: Is it ok if a lawyer gets Ford product?

parts.note: asking 'can I?' is asking whether it is ok if you do something
DA is a district attorney, an American prosecuting lawyer

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it is all right for an attorney to acquire a Ford car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ford product' suggests a car, but it is a novel by the American author Richard Ford.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Ford published the novel Canada in 2012, so it is literally a product of Ford's pen.

clue.text: Articles about Weller upset David's nephew

indicators.note: about means the two articles sit around the other piece

parts.note: A and A are two indefinite articles

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means the name is turned upside down, read bottom to top

parts.note: Sam Weller is Mr Pickwick's servant in Dickens's Pickwick Papers

explanation.surface: Grammar words about a man named Weller somehow upset a biblical relative.
explanation.walkthrough: Amasa is a minor biblical figure; in a down clue 'upset' reads the servant's name from bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible Amasa is the son of Abigail, sister of King David, making him the king's nephew.

clue.text: Do lancers put off animal-helping slave

indicators.note: put off here means disturbed or thrown into disorder, so the letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: A question whether cavalry soldiers would deter a slave who helps animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put off' rearranges the letters of DO LANCERS.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman tale, the runaway slave pulled a thorn from a lion's paw and was later spared by that grateful beast.

clue.text: Epic fail at centre involving nurse, earl and duke

indicators.note: involving means the middle letters enclose the following pieces
at centre asks for only the middle letters of the word fail

parts.note: EN is an enrolled nurse

explanation.surface: A heroic poem collapses in the middle while dragging in a nurse and two noblemen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Epic' looks like an adjective describing a fail, but it is the definition: Virgil's poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's poem about the wanderings of the Trojan hero is one of the great Latin epics.

clue.text: Perhaps Pyle's a chap seen around Morecambe?

indicators.note: seen around means the word for chap is wrapped round the comedian's first name

parts.note: a chap is a man
Eric Morecambe was a much-loved British comedian, half of Morecambe and Wise

explanation.surface: A man spotted near the seaside town of Morecambe is perhaps someone called Pyle.
explanation.walkthrough: Pyle is Alden Pyle, the title figure of Graham Greene's The Quiet American; Morecambe is also a Lancashire resort, which hides the comedian.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's Pyle is the young idealist from the United States in The Quiet American, an example of a US citizen.

clue.text: Surprisingly, warm to a real Self novel

indicators.note: surprisingly suggests the letters turn up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Will Self, the novelist, unexpectedly warms to a genuine version of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self' looks like the novelist Will Self, but it is only fodder; 'Surprisingly' rearranges all fifteen letters of WARM TO A REAL SELF.
explanation.definitionFit: Hemingway's 1929 book about an ambulance driver in the Italian campaign is a famous war novel.

clue.text: Aim consuming lean European like Albert Kropp?

indicators.note: consuming means the word for aim swallows the next pieces

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal
to list is to lean, as a ship does

explanation.surface: A goal swallowing a skinny European, someone like a character from a war novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Albert Kropp is a schoolboy who joins up in Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front.
explanation.definitionFit: Kropp and his classmates volunteer for the German army, so he is a soldier who signed up.

clue.text: State of Fingerbone Doggo had Indian nurses recoiling

indicators.note: recoiling means springing back, so the concealed letters are read backwards
nurses means holds within, so the letters are carried inside these words

explanation.surface: A dog in a novel's town was looked after by Indian nurses who shrank back.
explanation.walkthrough: Fingerbone is the lakeside town of Marilynne Robinson's Housekeeping. 'nurses' holds OHADI in 'Doggo had Indian', and 'recoiling' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Robinson's fictional Fingerbone lies in the US northwest, in the state whose capital is Boise.

clue.text: Book male into plant by hydro-electric construction?

indicators.note: into means the abbreviation goes inside the flower's name

parts.note: an aster is a daisy-like garden plant
a dam is built to drive a hydro-electric power station

explanation.surface: Instructions to schedule a man into a power plant next to a dam project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb meaning reserve, but it is the definition: Ian McEwan's Booker-winning novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan's 1998 novel, which won the Booker Prize, bears the name of the Dutch capital.

clue.text: Vernon's digs wound up everyone, daughter and Henry included

indicators.note: included means the daughter's letter is placed inside the phrase for teasing

parts.note: to wind someone up is British slang for teasing them, the same as having them on
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A young person's lodgings provoked everybody, with a daughter and a man named Henry sharing them.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorothy Vernon of Haddon Hall is a historical romance by Charles Major, set in the Derbyshire house where she lived.
explanation.definitionFit: The Derbyshire manor was the home of Dorothy Vernon, so it was her residence, informally her digs.

clue.text: When to get a hold of black English poet

indicators.note: to get a hold of means the word for when grips the next letter inside it

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A question of when to obtain a dark-skinned English poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Dannie Abse was a Welsh poet and doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Dannie Abse published many collections of verse, so he is a writer of verse.

clue.text: Beaufort scale applied to December air briefly?

parts.note: a carol is a song sung at Christmas, so a December tune
a piece written in the scale of E is said to be in E

explanation.surface: Applying the wind-force scale to a winter song, put briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beaufort scale is a measure of wind, but Beaufort is the definition: Caroline Beaufort, Victor's mother in Frankenstein. 'applied to' joins, and 'briefly' says the key is shortened to its letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In Mary Shelley's Frankenstein the hero's mother is born Caroline Beaufort, so her surname stands for her first name.

clue.text: Type who fires up horrific writer?

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys stirring up a horror author.
explanation.definitionFit: A boiler man feeds a furnace with fuel, and Bram Stoker wrote the horror novel Dracula.

clue.text: One's a ringer for one of the Bronte sisters

explanation.surface: A lookalike stands in for one of the famous literary sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: A church bell is rung, so it is something that rings; the sisters published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell.

clue.text: They rue an abominable musical work

indicators.note: abominable means dreadful or terrible, so these letters are wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: People regret a dreadful piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abominable' rearranges the letters of THEY RUE AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Weber's 1823 opera is a substantial piece of music for the stage.

clue.text: "Abide with me! Fast falls the -" (Henry Lyte)

definitions.text: "Abide with me! Fast falls the -" (Henry Lyte)

parts.words: "Abide with me! Fast falls the -" (Henry Lyte)
parts.note: the missing word completes the opening line of Henry Francis Lyte's famous hymn

explanation.surface: The opening line of a well-known hymn with its last word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyte's hymn begins with nightfall approaching, using an old poetic word for evening.

clue.text: As many Lovecraftian monsters and cattle end up

indicators.note: up here means stirred up or in disarray, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Like H.P. Lovecraft's creatures, livestock come to a bad end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' rearranges the letters of CATTLE END.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovecraft's horrors such as Cthulhu are famous for their writhing feelers, so they are described with this adjective.

clue.text: Hugh Stowell Scott is chap who's tipsy, I'm told

indicators.note: I'm told signals that the phrase is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: someone tipsy is merry, so a chap who has had a drink is a merry man

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist is reported to be a drunkard.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Stowell Scott wrote adventure novels under the pen name Henry Seton Merriman.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Hugh Stowell Scott published as Henry Seton Merriman, so the pseudonym's surname stands for him.

clue.text: In hearing, one supports Socialist writer

indicators.note: in hearing means the word is taken as it is heard spoken

parts.note: a trestle is a frame that supports a table top, one thing that holds up

explanation.surface: A listener backs a left-wing author.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Tressell wrote The Ragged-Trousered Philanthropists, a classic of socialist fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Tressell's novel about exploited house painters is a founding text of British left-wing literature.

clue.text: Captain old soldiers brought back to front

indicators.note: back to front means turned round, so the word for soldiers is read in reverse

parts.note: men are soldiers, the ranks as opposed to officers

explanation.surface: A captain's veteran troops were returned to the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Nemo commands the submarine Nautilus in Jules Verne; 'front' suggests a battlefield but belongs to 'back to front'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Verne's submarine commander in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea holds that naval rank.

clue.text: King's medal northern men returned

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so these letters are read in reverse, bottom to top here

parts.note: OR stands for other ranks, enlisted men

explanation.surface: A monarch's decoration given to northern soldiers who came home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns N and OR into RON. The 's of King's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: In A Midsummer Night's Dream he rules the fairies, so he is a monarch.

clue.text: Writer in The Tube taking the piss out of Alien

indicators.note: out of means the alien is taken away from the tube

parts.note: a catheter is a medical tube that drains urine from the bladder
ET is the extra-terrestrial of Spielberg's film, the classic crossword alien

explanation.surface: A writer on the London Underground mocks a creature from outer space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Tube' suggests the London Underground and 'taking the piss' British slang for mocking; together they describe a catheter. Willa Cather wrote My Antonia.
explanation.definitionFit: Willa Cather was an American novelist, author of O Pioneers! and My Antonia.

clue.text: Mythical shippropeller?

parts.note: a figure of legend whose face sent a thousand ships to sea, as if driving them like a propeller

explanation.definitionFit: Marlowe's Faustus calls her the face that launched a thousand ships, the fleet sailing to Troy for her.

clue.text: Novel concerned with a black horse?

parts.note: on means about or concerned with
Black Beauty is the horse of Anna Sewell's novel

explanation.surface: A story about a dark-coated horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is Zadie Smith's 2005 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Zadie Smith's 2005 book, set around a Boston college, is a work of fiction.

clue.text: Groan as American supports head of the Congress

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath the rest
head of asks for only the first letter of the following word

parts.note: it is a coy word for sex, and congress means sexual intercourse

explanation.surface: An American moans while holding up the leader of Congress.
explanation.walkthrough: Groan is a surname here: Titus Groan is the first of Mervyn Peake's Gormenghast novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Mervyn Peake's Gormenghast hero is the heir of the house of Groan, so his first name goes with that surname.

clue.text: It's found in Hamlet, Aladdin and others

indicators.note: found in signals letters sitting inside the run of the two titles

explanation.surface: A list of works including a tragedy and a pantomime, and more besides.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin abbreviation et al. stands for et alii, which translates as further people.

clue.text: Fantastic Templar-era religious satirist

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or unreal, so the letters are freely rearranged

explanation.surface: An imaginative mocker of the church from the age of the Knights Templar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic' rearranges TEMPLAR ERA. Martin Marprelate was the pen name behind Elizabethan pamphlets attacking bishops.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marprelate tracts of 1588-89 mocked the Anglican bishops, so their pseudonymous author was a satirist of the church.

clue.text: "Those who find ugly — in beautiful things are corrupt without being charming" (Oscar Wilde)

definitions.text: "Those who find ugly — in beautiful things are corrupt without being charming" (Oscar Wilde)

parts.words: "Those who find ugly — in beautiful things are corrupt without being charming" (Oscar Wilde)
parts.note: the missing word completes a line from Wilde's preface to The Picture of Dorian Gray

explanation.surface: A Wilde aphorism with one word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's preface says those who read unpleasant significance into lovely things are corrupt, so the gap is a word for senses.

clue.text: Detectives probing fruitcake, one committed to public exposure

indicators.note: probing means the detectives go inside the word for fruitcake

parts.note: fruitcake is slang for an eccentric, a nut
DIs are detective inspectors

explanation.surface: Police officers investigate a crank who flashes in public.
explanation.definitionFit: A naturist goes about unclothed, so is someone devoted to being seen bare.
